title: Load the hourly power file: one row per delivery hour, on one clock

explain.prompt: The trader looks at your table and asks two things. (1) “29 October 2023 has 25 rows — did the vendor send an hour twice?” (2) “I remember a 772 €/MWh print on 21 November 2023 at 18:00. Was that a spike?” Answer both in 4–6 sentences, with the numbers from your run, and say what would have gone wrong with a deduplication on `delivery_start_local` alone.
rubric: 29 Oct 2023 is the end of summer time: 02:00–03:00 local happens twice (+02:00 then +01:00). The two rows are two different delivery hours (00:00 and 01:00 UTC), not a duplicate — the day really has 25 hours (23 on the last Sunday of March).
Deduplicating on the local timestamp alone removes 11 rows instead of 9 and deletes the two genuine second 02:00 hours (2023 and 2024): load, generation and revenue for those hours disappear.
The vendor file has 17,553 rows: 6 exact copies (dropped) and 3 delivery hours sent in two versions; keeping the latest loaded_at leaves 17,544 hours = 727 days × 24 + 2 × 23 + 2 × 25.

21 Nov 2023 18:00: first loaded at 772.50 €/MWh, re-loaded two days later at 77.25 — a ×10 error corrected by the vendor. The trusted value is 77.25: it was not a spike, and keeping the first version would have created a fake one.

The two other revisions (a digit swap 23.82 → 32.82 on 12 Mar 2024 19:00, and a missing solar value filled in on 3 Jun 2024 13:00) show why the latest version must win — and why the number of revised records should be logged, not silently applied.
Every later calculation (daily averages, MWh, hour-of-day profiles) works on the UTC index; the local date and hour are labels, used only to group by market day.
